records.topic: The Tree That Blacked Out 56 Million Italians
records.coreQuestion: How did one power line touching a tree in Switzerland black out all of Italy?
records.openingLine: Why one Swiss tree blacked out 56 million.
records.secondBeat: In 2003, a Swiss line arced to a tree.
records.dependency: Italy's grid depended on imports over a few Alpine lines, protected by automatic relays.
records.mechanism: Relays trip lines that fault; neighbouring lines must carry the extra load within minutes.
records.bottleneck: Remaining lines could carry the load for only about 15 minutes.
records.failureConsequence: Operators didn't reduce imports fast enough, lines overheated and tripped in a cascade.
records.resilience: Better cross-border coordination and faster load reduction followed.
records.expectedConsequence: a whole country dark for up to 12 hours
editorialTitles: How One Tree Blacked Out Italy
Why Grids Have Only Minutes to React

facts.claim: The 2003 Italy blackout affected all of the Italian Peninsula for 12 hours and part of Switzerland near Geneva for 3 hours on 28 September 2003.
It was the largest blackout in the series of blackouts in 2003, involving about 56 million people.
The 400 kV Lukmanier powerline arced to a nearby tree and automatically disabled itself.
Those circuits could only stably carry the current for approximately 15 min, but the Swiss control room operator was not aware of the urgency.

narration.text: Why one Swiss tree blacked out 56 million.
In 2003, a Swiss line arced to a tree.
Other lines could carry its load for about 15 minutes.
The operator didn't grasp how little time there was.
Lines overheated and tripped one after another.
All of Italy lost power, some areas for 12 hours.
That's why cross-border grids run on minutes, not hours.

records.topic: The Spillway Failure That Evacuated 180,000 People
records.coreQuestion: How did damaged spillways at America's tallest dam force a mass evacuation?
records.secondBeat: In 2017, Oroville Dam's spillways both eroded.
records.dependency: Downstream towns depend on a dam's spillways safely releasing floodwater.
records.mechanism: Spillways carry excess water around the dam; if they erode, the dam's safety margin collapses.
records.bottleneck: Both the main and emergency spillways were damaged at once.
records.failureConsequence: Fears of an uncontrolled release forced evacuations downstream.
records.resilience: Emergency repairs and reduced lake levels averted disaster.
visualScenes: water pouring down the emergency spillway
editorialTitles: The Dam Crisis That Evacuated 180,000
Why Spillways Matter as Much as Dams

facts.claim: In early February 2017, Oroville Dam's main and emergency spillways both sustained damage during a period of sustained outflow from Lake Oroville, leading to the evacuation of areas downstream.
On February 13, authorities oversaw the evacuation of more than 180,000 people living in the threatened areas.
Completed in 1968, it is the tallest dam in the United States, at 770 feet (230 m).
It impounds Lake Oroville, capable of storing more than 3.5 million acre-feet (4.3 billion cubic meters).
Repairs to the dam were substantially complete by 2019.

narration.text: Why damaged spillways evacuated 180,000 people.
In 2017, Oroville Dam's spillways both eroded.
It's America's tallest dam, at 230 metres.
Its lake holds about 4.3 billion cubic metres.
Spillways are how a full reservoir safely lets water go.
Repairs weren't substantially complete until 2019.
That's why a dam is only as safe as its overflow.

records.topic: The Landfill Once the Largest in the World
records.coreQuestion: Where does a city of millions send its trash when its giant landfill closes?
records.openingLine: Why one landfill took 29,000 tons a day.
records.secondBeat: Fresh Kills was the world's largest landfill from 1955.
records.dependency: Cities depend on landfills or transfer stations to move thousands of tonnes of trash daily.
records.mechanism: Transfer stations consolidate collected waste into trucks, trains and barges bound for distant landfills.
records.bottleneck: When a single landfill closes, the whole flow must be rerouted.
records.failureConsequence: Transfer or export disruptions leave trash piling up on streets.
records.resilience: Multiple transfer stations and contracts spread the load.
records.expectedConsequence: waste costs rise as trash travels farther
visualScenes: trains hauling waste out of state
park being built on the old landfill
editorialTitles: Where a Megacity's Trash Goes
The Landfill That Was the World's Largest

facts.claim: The Fresh Kills Landfill was a landfill covering 2,200 acres (890 ha) in the borough of Staten Island in New York City.
The landfill opened in 1948, intended to be temporary, but by 1955 had become the largest in the world, and it remained so until its closure in 2001.
At the peak of its operation, in 1986, Fresh Kills received 29,000 short tons of residential waste per day.
From 1991 until its closing, it was the only landfill to accept New York City's residential waste.
It consists of four mounds that range in height from 90 to about 225 feet (30 to about 70 m).

narration.text: Why one landfill took 29,000 tons a day.
Fresh Kills was the world's largest landfill from 1955.
From 1991, it took all of New York's residential waste.
It closed in 2001.
The city's trash then had to leave by truck, train and barge.
Transfer stations now handle that daily flow.
That's why a city's cleanliness depends on where trash can go.

records.topic: The Policy That Upended Global Recycling
records.coreQuestion: What happened to recycling when China stopped accepting the world's scrap?
records.openingLine: Why a 0.5% rule upended global recycling.
records.secondBeat: China had been the main buyer of the world's scrap.
records.dependency: Many countries' recycling systems depended on exporting sorted scrap to China.
records.mechanism: Recovery facilities sort mixed recyclables into bales sold to overseas processors.
records.bottleneck: China's contamination limit dropped to 0.5%, far below what many facilities could reach.
records.failureConsequence: Bales piled up and some recycling went to landfill.
records.resilience: Better sorting and new domestic processors slowly followed.
records.expectedConsequence: recycling costs rise and some programmes shrink
visualScenes: sorting line at a recycling facility
bales of mixed paper stacked up
editorialTitles: The Day China Stopped Taking Our Recycling
Why Recycling Depends on Clean Sorting

facts.claim: The Operation National Sword (ONS) was a policy initiative launched in 2017 by the government of China to monitor and more stringently review recyclable waste imports.
The Chinese government also announced that the percentage of contaminants allowed in recycled materials would drop from 5–10% to 0.5%.
In March 2018, the National Sword policy came into effect, banning the import of 24 categories of scrap materials, including low-grade plastics and unsorted mixed paper.
China had first brought awareness of its intention to limit its imports of contaminated waste and recyclables back in 2013, through its Operation Green Fence program.
China notified the World Trade Organization on 18 July 2017 that it intended to ban additional solid waste imports by year-end.
By early 2019, many Southeast Asian countries also started to reject the waste as well.

narration.text: Why a 0.5% rule upended global recycling.
China had been the main buyer of the world's scrap.
It cut allowed contamination from 5–10% to just 0.5%.
It followed an earlier 2013 crackdown called Green Fence.
Its 2018 ban covered 24 categories of scrap.
Other Asian countries soon began rejecting it too.
Sorting facilities suddenly needed near-perfect bales.
That's why recycling is only as good as the sorting line.

records.topic: The Milk Scandal That Sickened 300,000 Children
records.coreQuestion: How did melamine in baby formula sicken hundreds of thousands of children?
records.secondBeat: In 2008, melamine was added to Chinese dairy products.
records.dependency: Food safety depends on laboratories testing for contaminants, not just the nutrients they claim.
records.mechanism: Tests measured nitrogen to estimate protein; melamine faked high protein readings.
records.bottleneck: Standard tests weren't looking for melamine.
records.failureConsequence: Contaminated formula reached infants across China.
records.resilience: Testing for melamine became mandatory worldwide.
records.expectedConsequence: mass illness and a collapse of trust in dairy
editorialTitles: The Formula Scandal That Fooled Food Tests
Why Food Labs Must Test for the Unexpected

facts.claim: 300,000 affected children were identified, among which 54,000 were hospitalized, according to the latest report in January 2009.
The culprit, melamine, was undetected in the tests until 1 August.
Further government inspections revealed that products from 21 other companies were also tainted.
New Zealand dairy giant Fonterra, which owned a 43% stake in Sanlu, were alerted to the contamination on 2 August.

narration.text: Why tainted milk sickened 300,000 children.
In 2008, melamine was added to Chinese dairy products.
Tests estimated protein from nitrogen, and melamine faked it.
About 54,000 children were hospitalised.
Products from 21 more companies were found tainted.
Labs had not been looking for melamine at all.
That's why food safety depends on testing for the unexpected.

records.topic: The Beef Burgers That Were 100% Horse
records.coreQuestion: How did horse meat end up sold as beef across Europe?
records.secondBeat: In 2013, DNA tests exposed it across Europe.
records.dependency: Consumers and retailers depend on traceability to know what's really in processed meat.
records.mechanism: Meat passes through traders and processors across borders before reaching products.
records.bottleneck: Long, multi-country chains made substitution hard to detect.
records.failureConsequence: DNA tests revealed horse meat in products labelled beef.
records.resilience: More DNA testing and supply-chain audits followed.
records.expectedConsequence: mass recalls and lost trust in processed meat
editorialTitles: The Scandal Hidden in Europe's Beef
Why DNA Tests Rewrote Food Labels

facts.claim: The crisis escalated in February 2013 when some Findus products were found to contain up to 100% horsemeat instead of beef.
The analysis found that 23 out of 27 beef burger samples also contained pig DNA.
The scandal later spread to 13 other European countries.
The first positive test for equine DNA was on 10 December 2012.

narration.text: Why some 'beef' meals were 100% horse.
In 2013, DNA tests exposed it across Europe.
23 of 27 burger samples also contained pig DNA.
The scandal spread to 13 more European countries.
Meat passed through traders in several countries before packing.
Each hand-off was a chance to swap what's inside.
That's why food labels are only as true as their traceability.

records.topic: The Formula Shortage That Emptied 70% of Shelves
records.coreQuestion: How did one plant's shutdown leave most U.S. baby formula shelves empty?
records.openingLine: Why 70% of formula shelves went empty.
records.secondBeat: In 2022, America's biggest formula plant shut down.
records.dependency: U.S. families depended on a few producers, with one firm making 40% of formula.
records.mechanism: Lean inventories keep costs down but leave little buffer when a plant stops.
records.bottleneck: Abbott's Sturgis plant was its largest, and few others could ramp up quickly.
records.failureConsequence: After a recall and plant closure, out-of-stock rates hit 70%.
records.resilience: Imports and emergency airlifts refilled shelves over months.
records.expectedConsequence: parents search store to store for formula
editorialTitles: The Baby Formula Crisis Explained
Why Lean Supply Chains Leave Shelves Empty

facts.claim: On May 14, nationwide out-of-stock rates were reported to be 43%, up from 31% two weeks prior; by May 22, they had surged to 70%.
facts.source: Wikipedia — 2022 United States infant formula shortage

facts.claim: Abbott produces 40% of the formula sold in the US, mostly under the Similac brand, and the Sturgis facility is its largest.
facts.source: Wikipedia — 2022 United States infant formula shortage

facts.claim: This is drastically above normal out-of-stock rates of 10%, or reported in the first half of 2021, 2% to 8%.
facts.source: Wikipedia — 2022 United States infant formula shortage

facts.claim: The FDA did not inspect the plant until January 31, 2022.
facts.source: Wikipedia — 2022 United States infant formula shortage

narration.text: Why 70% of formula shelves went empty.
In 2022, America's biggest formula plant shut down.
Abbott makes about 40% of U.S. formula.
Out-of-stock rates jumped from 31% to 70% in weeks.
Normally, that rate sits around 10%.
The FDA hadn't inspected the plant until January 31, 2022.
Lean stock and few suppliers left no buffer.
That's why safety stock is cheap insurance.

records.topic: The GPS Clock That Resets Every 1,024 Weeks
records.coreQuestion: Why does GPS time roll back to zero every 19.6 years?
records.openingLine: Why GPS time resets every 1,024 weeks.
records.dependency: GPS receivers depend on a week counter in the satellite message to work out the date.
records.mechanism: The legacy message stores the week number in just ten bits, counting 0 to 1,023.
records.bottleneck: After week 1,023, the counter overflows to zero.
records.failureConsequence: Receivers not built for the rollover can jump back about 20 years.
records.resilience: Newer GPS signals use a 13-bit counter; firmware updates handle rollovers.
records.expectedConsequence: old devices show wrong dates or stop working
visualScenes: GPS receiver showing a wrong date
editorialTitles: Why GPS Time Rolls Back Every 19.6 Years
The 10-Bit Counter Hidden in GPS

facts.claim: The GPS week number rollover is a phenomenon that happens every 1,024 weeks, or about 19.6 years.
The GPS message broadcasts a date which includes a week number counter stored in only ten binary digits, whose range is therefore 0–1,023.
Software that is not coded to anticipate the rollover to zero may stop working or could be moved back in time by a multiple of approximately 20 years.
The new CNAV format has a 13-bit week number counter in the range of 0–8191.

narration.text: Why GPS time resets every 1,024 weeks.
That's about every 19.6 years.
The week number fits in just ten binary digits.
After week 1,023, it rolls back to zero.
Unprepared devices can jump back about 20 years.
Newer signals count up to 8,191 weeks.
Clocks in networks and ships read that date too.
That's why tiny design choices echo for decades.

records.topic: The Trading Glitch That Lost $460 Million
records.coreQuestion: How did one software deployment error nearly destroy a major trading firm?
records.openingLine: Why one glitch cost Knight Capital $460 million.
records.secondBeat: In 2012, it handled 17.3% of NYSE trading.
records.dependency: Markets depend on trading firms' automated systems behaving exactly as intended.
records.mechanism: Algorithms send orders at machine speed; a faulty deployment can flood markets with trades.
records.bottleneck: Errors compound in minutes before humans can react.
records.failureConsequence: Knight Capital lost $460 million and had to be acquired.
records.resilience: Kill switches and deployment controls became standard.
records.expectedConsequence: a firm's capital evaporates before anyone can stop it
editorialTitles: The Trading Glitch That Sank a Firm
Why Trading Software Needs a Kill Switch

facts.claim: The company agreed to be acquired by Getco LLC in December 2012 after an August 2012 trading error lost $460 million.
Knight had a market share of 17.3% on NYSE and 16.9% on NASDAQ.
Its Electronic Trading Group covered more than 19,000 U.S. securities with an average daily trading volume of more than 21 billion dollars in May 2012.
The merger was completed in July 2013, forming KCG Holdings.

narration.text: Why one glitch cost Knight Capital $460 million.
In 2012, it handled 17.3% of NYSE trading.
It traded more than $21 billion a day.
A faulty software rollout sent a flood of unwanted orders.
By December, it agreed to be acquired.
Machines trade faster than people can react.
That's why trading systems need a hard stop button.

records.topic: The Two-Digit Bug That Cost $300 Billion to Fix
records.coreQuestion: Why did the world spend over $300 billion fixing two missing digits?
records.openingLine: Why fixing two digits cost over $300 billion.
records.dependency: Banks, utilities and governments depended on old software storing years as two digits.
records.bottleneck: The bug was buried across millions of lines of legacy code.
records.failureConsequence: Unfixed systems could miscalculate interest, dates and schedules.
records.resilience: Years of remediation meant few major errors occurred.
records.expectedConsequence: a quiet New Year thanks to expensive preparation
visualScenes: COBOL code on a green screen
editorialTitles: The Y2K Bug That Didn't Happen
Why Fixing Two Digits Cost $300 Billion

facts.claim: The Year 2000 problem (Y2K) was the potential for computer errors related to the formatting and storage of calendar data for dates in and after the year 2000.
Storing 1985 as 85 made the year 2000 indistinguishable from 1900.
The total cost of the work done in preparation for Y2K likely surpassed US$300 billion.
IDC calculated that the US spent an estimated $134 billion preparing for Y2K, and another $13 billion fixing problems in 2000 and 2001.
Contrary to published expectations, few major errors occurred in 2000.

narration.text: Why fixing two digits cost over $300 billion.
Old systems stored 1985 simply as 85.
So 2000 looked the same as 1900.
America alone spent about $134 billion preparing.
Few major errors happened in 2000.
The quiet New Year was the result of years of repairs.
That's why bank ledgers still carry decisions made decades ago.

records.topic: The Mine Worth 2.5% of Chile's Economy
records.coreQuestion: Why does one copper mine in the desert matter to the global economy?
records.openingLine: Why one mine makes 2.5% of Chile's GDP.
records.secondBeat: Escondida is a giant copper pit 3,100 metres up.
records.dependency: Wiring, motors and grids worldwide depend on copper concentrate from a few giant mines.
records.mechanism: Ore is mined, concentrated and shipped to smelters, largely in China.
records.bottleneck: A handful of giant mines supply a large share of copper.
records.failureConsequence: Strikes or outages at one mine move world copper prices.
records.resilience: Recycling and other mines cover part of any shortfall.
records.expectedConsequence: copper prices spike when a giant mine stops
visualScenes: open-pit mine terraces in the Atacama
editorialTitles: The Desert Mine Powering the World's Wires
Why One Copper Mine Moves Markets

facts.claim: Escondida is a large open-pit copper mine at 3,100 m (10,200 ft) elevation in the Atacama Desert in Antofagasta Region, Chile.
In 2019 it was estimated that the mine and its ancillary industries generated 2.5% of Chile's GDP.
Total resources (including reserves) were 57.6 million tonnes of copper, of which 33.0 million tonnes should be recovered.
The mine's produce is largely exported to China as ore concentrate.

narration.text: Why one mine makes 2.5% of Chile's GDP.
Escondida is a giant copper pit 3,100 metres up.
It holds about 57.6 million tonnes of copper.
Most of its concentrate ships to China for smelting.
A few mines like it supply much of the world's copper.
A strike there can move copper prices worldwide.
That's why the world's wiring starts in a desert pit.

records.topic: The Smelter Using 13% of a Country's Electricity
records.coreQuestion: Why does one aluminium smelter use 13% of New Zealand's electricity?
records.openingLine: Why one smelter uses 13% of national power.
records.secondBeat: Tiwai Point opened in 1971, with its own hydro station.
records.dependency: Aluminium smelting depends on huge amounts of cheap, reliable electricity.
records.mechanism: Electrolysis splits alumina into aluminium, drawing power around the clock.
records.bottleneck: One plant's demand is a large share of a national grid.
records.failureConsequence: Closing it would shake the power market and the regional economy.
records.resilience: Long-term power contracts keep the plant running.
records.expectedConsequence: power prices and jobs swing on one plant's future
visualScenes: hydro station built to supply it
editorialTitles: The Smelter That Uses 13% of a Country's Power
Why Aluminium Is Frozen Electricity

facts.claim: It uses 13 percent of New Zealand's electricity, and is reported to account for 10 percent of the Southland region's economy.
The smelter was opened in 1971 following the construction of the Manapouri Power Station by the New Zealand government to supply it with electricity.
Rio Tinto has threatened to close the smelter several times, for example in 2013 and 2020.
In May 2024, new twenty-year electricity contracts were agreed with three suppliers, allowing the smelter to remain open until 2044.

narration.text: Why one smelter uses 13% of national power.
Tiwai Point opened in 1971, with its own hydro station.
It's about 10% of the Southland region's economy.
Its owner threatened closure in 2013 and again in 2020.
New contracts now keep it open until 2044.
Aluminium smelting runs on electricity around the clock.
That's why aluminium is sometimes called frozen electricity.

records.topic: The Outage That Cut Off 10 Million Australians
records.coreQuestion: How did one network change cut internet and phones for 10 million Australians?
records.openingLine: Why 10 million Australians lost service at once.
records.secondBeat: In 2023, all Optus services went down at 4:05 a.m.
records.dependency: Mobile, broadband and business services depend on a carrier's core routing staying stable.
records.mechanism: Routers exchange routing updates; a bad update can make them disconnect to protect themselves.
records.bottleneck: One carrier served about a quarter of Australian mobile users.
records.failureConsequence: All services went down at once, for hours.
records.resilience: Engineers restored service by resetting routers, gradually.
records.expectedConsequence: businesses, payments and emergency contact disrupted nationwide
editorialTitles: How 10 Million Australians Lost Service
Why One Carrier Outage Can Stop a Country

facts.claim: On 8 November 2023, an unplanned network outage occurred, consisting of all Optus internet, cellular and fixed-line services in Australia at 04:05 AEDT.
The outage directly affected more than 10 million people and 400,000 businesses across Australia.
Around 25% of Australians use Optus for their cellular service and 19% for broadband internet.
Restoration was gradual with some services being restored around 13:00 AEDT.

narration.text: Why 10 million Australians lost service at once.
In 2023, all Optus services went down at 4:05 a.m.
About 400,000 businesses were affected.
Around 25% of Australians use it for mobile service.
Some services only returned around 1 p.m.
A core routing fault took every service down together.
That's why one carrier's control room is national infrastructure.

records.topic: The Test Tool That Misshaped Hubble's Mirror
records.coreQuestion: How did a badly assembled test device ruin the Hubble Space Telescope's first images?
records.openingLine: Why Hubble's mirror was 2,200 nanometres off.
records.secondBeat: It was polished smooth to about 10 nanometres.
records.dependency: Precision optics depend on calibration instruments that tell makers when a surface is right.
records.mechanism: A null corrector guides mirror polishing; if it's wrong, the mirror is made perfectly wrong.
records.bottleneck: One test instrument was trusted without independent cross-checks.
records.failureConsequence: The mirror's edge was 2,200 nanometres too flat, blurring images.
records.resilience: A 1993 servicing mission added corrective optics.
records.expectedConsequence: a flagship telescope launched with blurred vision
visualScenes: mirror polishing in a clean room
editorialTitles: The Calibration Error That Blurred Hubble
Why Measuring Tools Need Checking Too

facts.claim: Although it was believed to be one of the most precisely figured optical mirrors ever made, smooth to about 10 nanometers, the outer perimeter was too flat by about 2200 nanometers.
The Allen Commission found that a reflective null corrector, a testing device used to achieve a properly shaped non-spherical mirror, had been incorrectly assembled.
Hubble features a 2.4 m (7 ft 10 in) mirror.
The optics were corrected to their intended quality by a servicing mission, STS-61, in 1993.
The Hubble Space Telescope was launched into low Earth orbit in 1990 and remains in operation.

narration.text: Why Hubble's mirror was 2,200 nanometres off.
It was polished smooth to about 10 nanometres.
But its outer edge was ground too flat.
The test device guiding the polishing was assembled wrong.
Hubble launched in 1990 with blurred vision.
Its main mirror is 2.4 metres across.
Astronauts fitted corrective optics in 1993.
That's why the tools that measure need measuring too.
